cur:objects-sinai-abgar-mandylion-tripty.summary: On the upper part of the right wing King Abgar of Edessa, enthroned and crowned, holds out the Mandylion — the cloth bearing the face of Christ — while the apostle Thaddeus appears on the left wing; below stand monastic saints. The holy face on the cloth, the 'image not made by hands', is the true focus of the scene. The panels celebrate the arrival of this relic in Constantinople in 944 and the belief that Christ himself had left his likeness to the world.
facts: Wikipedia records that the Image of Edessa was brought to Constantinople in 944, after the city was besieged by John Kourkouas and the cloth was exchanged for Muslim prisoners.
The legend held that Abgar, king of Edessa, had written to Christ asking to be healed and received in reply a cloth miraculously imprinted with his face — the Mandylion (tradition).
cur:objects-sinai-abgar-mandylion-tripty.notes: Abgar is often said to bear the features of Emperor Constantine VII (an interpretation, not a documented fact). A public-domain detail of Abgar with the Mandylion is 'Abgarwithimageofedessa10thcentury.jpg'.

cur:objects-khanenko-sergius-bacchus-ico.summary: The soldier-martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, wearing the gold torques of the imperial guard and holding small crosses, look out side by side with wide, calm eyes. Between their haloes a small medallion shows the bearded face of Christ, the Lord for whom they gave their lives. The icon expresses the bond between Christ and his martyrs in the intimate, luminous manner of the earliest encaustic icons.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the Khanenko Museum holds four early Byzantine encaustic icons of the 6th and 7th centuries — among them this one — which came to the museum in 1940 and have been displayed in a dedicated room since 2004.
cur:objects-khanenko-sergius-bacchus-ico.notes: These icons are widely reported to have been brought from Sinai by the Russian bishop Porfiry Uspensky in the 19th century; not confirmed in the source read here.
